rationale: Today's slate stays on plague. The long video is an evergreen case study built on one primary source: CDC's MMWR report (Feb 25, 2011) on the fatal lab-acquired infection in Chicago in 2009. It's well documented and few channels cover it. It also adds something new to our lab-safety coverage, because the Oct 9 long video explained general biosafety levels and this one is a single case. Fast-moving news stays out of the long video. The breaking-news angle goes into a Short instead: a dated status decoder that opens with WHO's Oct 10 statement that the cause is still unclear. The playbook names this exact format. S2 is a spin-off of L1 to send viewers to the long video. S3 answers the newest search question ("why don't they know yet?") using CDC's presumptive vs confirmed case definition. It's an emerging topic with little competition. The carousel quota is a myths-vs-facts list that corrects beliefs already circulating, each with the agency that answers it. That's the contrarian slot, and a list format is the best chance for a carousel to get saves. The mix is two emerging, one rising/peaking (status), the evergreen case-study long video with a timely hook, and one myth-busting piece. Topics vary across the day: the news, a lab case study with iron overload in the blood, lab diagnostics, and myths. No body system gets three pieces. Every title starts with "Plague", contains no fear words, and carries the dated hedge and the urgent-contact line. The pillar list only has GLP-1 playlists, so every piece goes to 'general' (Health Science Explained), the only playlist that fits plague content.

pieces.topic: Lab-acquired plague in the US: the fatal 2009 Chicago case of a researcher infected with a weakened (attenuated) Yersinia pestis strain who had undiagnosed hereditary hemochromatosis (CDC MMWR, Feb 25, 2011)
pieces.angle: A calm, well-documented case study built only on the CDC MMWR report (and the CDC Stacks record). At most one neutral line of news context ('plague has been in the news this month'), with no claims about the Irkutsk case. Don't lead with the researcher's name. Segments: (1) What an attenuated strain is and why this one was considered lower-risk (it lacks the pigmentation locus, so it depends on iron). (2) The timeline and clinical course in MMWR's wording. (3) How the investigation found hereditary hemochromatosis (iron overload) and why it's thought to have let the weakened strain cause severe infection. Use MMWR's hedged verbs such as 'might have' or 'likely'. (4) CDC's conclusion: likely an unrecognized occupational exposure, with no clear route identified. Keep MMWR's exact scope. (5) Contact follow-up and preventive antibiotics as MMWR reports them; no secondary cases. (6) What MMWR recommended for labs: awareness, reporting exposures and illness, and medical follow-up. Mention BMBL practices (updated Mar 18, 2026) only in that source's own words. (7) What it means for the public: plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early' (CDC). Close: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Then 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Visuals: lab scene, iron-in-blood diagram, timeline cards. No patient imagery, skulls or rats.
pieces.working_title: Plague in a US Lab: What CDC Learned From a 2009 Chicago Case
pieces.why: A deep primary source (CDC MMWR) that can be checked line by line. Interest is new (Céline Gounder's Oct 10 comparison), competition is low, and the body doesn't depend on unresolved news, which is what keeps holding plague long videos.

pieces.topic: Plague status decoder, as of Oct 12, 2026: what's confirmed, reported and still unknown about the Irkutsk oblast lab worker's death
pieces.angle: Open (as of Oct 12, 2026): 'On Oct 10, WHO said a key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker' (WHO Disease Outbreak News). Then, credited and dated, in this order. Oct 6: WHO (Lindmeier), word for word: 'No cause of death has been officially confirmed to date and laboratory testing is reportedly underway.' Oct 8: Rospotrebnadzor 'rejected reports about a second person falling ill' (AP), and WHO asked about a reported second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause (Tedros). Oct 8–9: Irkutsk oblast governor Igor Kobzev reported about 5,000 lab tests with no dangerous pathogens and lifted restrictions; AP noted he did not explicitly say whether pneumonic plague had been ruled out. Oct 10: Russia's IHR focal point told WHO that no case of plague has been registered recently in Irkutsk Oblast and called the death 'pneumonia of undetermined etiology'; WHO said it has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission based on that information, and requested more lab and contact details. End on WHO still asking for confirmation of the diagnosis. Introduce her as 'a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died'. Close with 'If you have possible exposure and symptoms, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently' and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Plague in Russia: What's Confirmed vs Suspected (as of Oct 12, 2026) #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Plague in Russia: What's Confirmed vs Suspected (as of Oct 12, 2026) #shorts
pieces.why: WHO's Oct 10 'cause still unclear' statement is under 48 hours old, and the playbook names the dated decoder as the breaking-news Short format. The news angle stays in a Short and out of the long video. | fact-check: I verified a newer, primary source: WHO Disease Outbreak News DON620, 'Pneumonia of undetermined etiology - the Russian Federation', published Oct 10, 2026 (https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON620). The opening beat should credit this, not Reuters/CBC paraphrase. The DON says Russia's IHR National Focal Point told WHO 'no case of plague has been registered recently in Irkutsk Oblast', that there were no biosafety incidents, that contacts tested negative for high-threat pathogens, and that the death was 'pneumonia of undetermined etiology'. WHO: 'A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.' WHO also says it 'has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event' based on information from the NFP. AP (Oct 10) quotes a different WHO line: 'Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment.' Reports differ on test counts: the governor's figure was about 5,000, and AP on Oct 10 reported more than 5,500. Credit each figure to whoever said it and when, or drop the number. Every line must be credited to the body that said it, at its exact scope. The NFP's statement is Russia's claim relayed by WHO, not WHO's own finding. Never say 'ruled out' or 'not plague'. Re-check WHO, Rospotrebnadzor and CDC at publish time, because the DON may be updated. Keep 170 words or fewer: cut the Axios CDC line before cutting any dated WHO line.

pieces.topic: Why a weakened plague strain turned deadly: iron overload (hereditary hemochromatosis) in the 2009 Chicago lab case (CDC MMWR)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Plague and Iron: How a Weakened Strain May Have Caused a Fatal Case (CDC) #shorts'. Answer within 10 s: 'This 2009 lab strain was weakened: it lacks genes it uses to grab iron. CDC says the researcher's undiagnosed iron overload (hereditary hemochromatosis) might have supplied enough iron to overcome that defect.' Then CDC's findings: the exposure route was undetermined (a respiratory route could not be ruled out definitively), and close contacts got preventive antibiotics with no additional infections identified. Close: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC). Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Point viewers to L1. 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: Plague and Iron: Why a Weakened Strain Turned Deadly (CDC) #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It teases the surprising iron detail and sends viewers to the full case-study video. | fact-check: The science is verified in the same MMWR (mm6007a1): a pgm- KIM D27 strain with iron-acquisition defects, and hemochromatosis that 'might have provided' enough iron. The working title 'Why a Weakened Strain Turned Deadly' states a cause outright, which MMWR only hedges. That is the causal-title problem that held S2 09-30. 'Turned deadly' also suggests the strain changed. The strain stayed attenuated; the host's iron overload is the proposed factor. Keep the respiratory-route caveat if the route comes up. Don't name the person and don't draw any link to Irkutsk.

pieces.topic: Plague testing explained: what 'presumptive' vs 'confirmed' plague means under CDC's 2020 case definition, and why confirmation can take days
pieces.angle: Hook: 'Plague tests: why can confirming it take days?' Context line (one sentence): 'As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO says a key uncertainty in the Irkutsk oblast death is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis.' Then settled science only: under CDC's 2020 case definition, PCR, antigen or F1 rapid tests make a case presumptive or probable; confirmed means Y. pestis grown in culture or a fourfold change in antibody levels between samples. Culture and paired antibody tests take time, which is why clinicians start antibiotics before results are back when plague is suspected. Close: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently; 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Plague Tests: Why Confirming It Can Take Days (CDC) #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Plague Tests: Why Confirming It Can Take Days (CDC) #shorts
pieces.why: It answers today's top new search question (NYT, Oct 10) with settled CDC definitions and no speculation. Low competition, and it doubles as the playbook's 35–50 s length test. | fact-check: The topic is settled science and on-format: a plain question, an agency named, and 'Plague' as the first word. Swap the context line for the primary-source wording: WHO DON620 (Oct 10, 2026) says 'A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.' Don't use 'WHO said the cause is still unclear' from news paraphrase. Follow the craft-note rules: PCR, antigen and F1 rapid tests = 'presumptive/probable'; 'confirmed' = Y. pestis isolated in culture or a fourfold change in antibody titer. Cite the CDC/CSTE case definition page itself (NNDSS Plague 2020 case definition), not the 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis' page. Don't give specific culture turnaround hours unless a cited source states them. Antibody fourfold rises need paired samples taken weeks apart. Say 'can take days or longer' rather than a fixed figure. Don't imply that any specific test was or wasn't done in the Irkutsk case. 35–50 s is fine.

pieces.topic: Plague myths vs facts: 6 beliefs circulating now, each corrected by the agency that answers it
pieces.angle: Slide 1: 'Plague: 6 myths vs what CDC and WHO say', with the status line 'As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO: a key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the Irkutsk oblast death (WHO Disease Outbreak News).' Myths: (1) Extinct → CDC's live US wording at publish time ('an average of five human plague cases are reported each year', range 0–17). (2) No cure → CDC: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.' (3) Airborne like COVID or measles → CDC: pneumonic plague 'requires direct and close contact'; infected people or animals 'can sometimes cough droplets'. (4) All plague spreads between people → CDC: 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people' (CDC How Plague Spreads), with no added absolute in our voice. (5) Home antibiotics protect me → health authorities give close contacts a 7-day preventive course (WHO); don't self-treat or stockpile. (6) Only rats → wild rodents and their fleas, and pets can carry fleas home (CDC); 'follow the label; some dog flea products (e.g. permethrin) are toxic to cats'. Final slide: CDC's 4 pneumonic signs (fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain); possible exposure means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently; 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' No bioweapon or lab-leak myths.
pieces.working_title: Plague: 6 Myths vs What CDC and WHO Actually Say
pieces.why: The myth-busting slot. It corrects beliefs already spreading ('no cure', 'airborne like COVID', 'extinct') in a save-and-share list. Every correction uses an agency's exact wording. | fact-check: The myth corrections are sound, but four fixes are needed. (1) Myth 4, 'only pneumonic spreads between people': quote CDC's droplet sentence exactly and credit it to CDC How Plague Spreads (updated May 15, 2024). Don't turn it into an absolute in our own voice, because WHO's fact sheet (updated Sep 29, 2026) notes rare person-to-person spread outside the pneumonic form, e.g. via infected material. Use 'Rare' plus WHO's wording if you include it. (2) Myth 3: say 'not airborne like measles' only via CDC's 'requires direct and close contact' and 'can sometimes cough droplets'. Keep 'sometimes' and the animal half. Don't say 'not contagious'. (3) The slide 1 status line must use WHO's Oct 10 DON wording, not 'WHO says the cause is still unclear; plague not confirmed' in our own voice. (4) Myth 5: credit preventive antibiotics to health authorities (WHO: 'seven-day chemoprophylaxis' for contacts), with no drug names or doses. Format note from the playbook: all 13 carousels reached 0–2 accounts, so the owner should consider rebuilding this as a Short. The topic itself is safe and approved with these fixes.
